title: Produced Water Treatment: From Reuse to What’s Next | Episode 10
summary: Produced water treatment and logistics create options, from recycling in completions to beneficial reuse and minerals. Key takeaways from The Water Exchange.
body_markdown:
[Produced water treatment](https://www.selectwater.com/produced-water-recycling-in-the-permian/) , paired with the logistics to store and move water, gives produced water optionality. That idea ran through Episode 10 of[The Water Exchange](https://www.selectwater.com/category/podcast/) , where Rick McCurdy, vice president of innovation and sustainability at Select Water Solutions, sat down with Aaron Horn, vice president of infrastructure for New Mexico. Tune in as they trace produced water recycling from early shale projects to fracs that can run on 100% recycled water, and on to what’s next for the industry.


## Key Takeaways


### Logistics and Bacteria Control Make Produced Water Recycling Work


Produced water treatment for recycling follows a fairly standard routine: oxidize the water, remove solids, sometimes filter it, and send it to a pit. What sets a network apart is scale and connectivity, gathering water from many operators and moving it to wherever a frac is running. Once the water is in the pond, bacteria is the daily challenge, not salt. Polymer chemistry changed the game when friction reducers that work in salt water replaced guar gels, so salt no longer limits recycling.


### Disposal Remains the Backstop


Recycling serves fracs, but the network still needs[disposal](https://www.selectwater.com/water/gathering-disposal/) so it can keep taking water without shutting in oil-producing wells. Studies suggest Permian disposal capacity could run short in the coming years, which makes alternatives to disposal a priority.


### Produced Water Treatment for Beneficial Reuse Starts With Salt


When the industry looks to put produced water to work beyond frac recycling, salt becomes the real hurdle. Removing dissolved salt is a step change in cost, scope, and capital compared with controlling solids and bacteria.


### Minerals, Cooling, and Power Widen the Optionality


Produced water can be more than a frac input. Select’s treatment and connected network let the same barrel serve a different operator’s frac across the basin, cooling for data centers and power generation, or mineral extraction, with disposal as the backstop. Demand is growing in places short on both power and fresh water, like Southeastern New Mexico, and Select is already working with lithium extraction companies and has entered an agreement with an iodine extraction company. Treatment is what keeps those options open.


When operators, neighbors, regulators, and communities see produced water as a resource rather than a waste, behavior follows. Press play on the full episode to hear how Rick and Aaron get into all of it, and find the full transcript below.


### Full Transcript


*This transcript has been lightly edited for readability.*


Welcome everybody to the Water Exchange podcast. I’m Rick McCurdy, vice president of innovation and sustainability with Select Water Solutions. And I’m Aaron Horn, vice president of infrastructure for New Mexico for Select Water Solutions. Hey, Aaron. I’d like to kick off with… You and I have a history that go back somewhat. I first became aware of you when you were an engineer for Newfield, and y’all were doing some produced water treatment. I believe it was in the Woodford Shale And doing some surface discharge, which was allowed in Oklahoma per the Corporation Commission rules.


And you had written an SPE paper about that and I remember downloading and reading an SPE paper when I was at Chesapeake. So that would have been seventeen years ago. Seventeen years ago. Not long after that, the treatment company that we used on that project recruited me out of my cushy engineering position at the time. And I started working for a smaller company and helped them sell. And my very first sales pitch was to Rick McCurdy of Chesapeake and you frightened the hell out of me. I remember getting into the elevator with you and you’re so polite and nice and we went down the elevator into this big room and started giving my pitch and you politely started picking me apart.


This is how this is always gonna go. I’m in serious trouble. Well, it wasn’t mean spirited. Oh, no. No. No. I was… Just how it was, and I remember that. I remember that activity. That was fun. But, again, listen, that was enough reminiscing. Let’s talk about where we’re at today. And, obviously, you’re over in the Delaware Basin, right, over in Carlsbad? I am. And we… Let’s go ahead and do talk a little bit about history. We do that all the time, you know, when it comes to produced water treatment. You know, back when we were first getting going into business, I mean, it’s freshwater everywhere.


And much smaller fracs even with the unconventionals. You know, these were typically, you know, maybe three, 400,000 barrels tops. And, of course, the reuse really got underway up in the Marcellus just because the cost of having to dispose of water up there… Because they had to. But Newfield was one of the leaders, particularly in Oklahoma, in reusing produced water. You wanna talk about that a little bit? Gosh. Again, this was in 2009, 2007 to 2009. And so we had a shortage of surface groundwater In the area where we were fracking.


And we were fracking in Central Oklahoma, Woodford Shale, gas play, and we were just running out of water. Was there was no aquifer water there. So we had to find a way to find more water. So some folks said, hey, let’s try to use our produced water. And I mean, that was the beginning of my involvement in produced water recycling. At the time we would recycle maybe 10% of the frac volume would be produced water. And now our customers today, usually 95 plus percent, sometimes a 100% of their half million barrel fracs compared to our 100,000 barrel fracs in the Woodford in Central Oklahoma.


Half million barrel fracs, 100% recycled produced water. So that’s what nineteen years has evolved into. And of course, now you look at where we’re at today, you know, like I said, much smaller fracs back then. Now we’re typically on a single well somewhere in the neighborhood of three quarters of a million barrels per well on that. And then now we’ve got the advent of simul fracs. First, was zipper fracs, now simul fracs, now trimul fracs. How’s that affecting your business? So in two ways, it certainly impacts our planning, but it also gives us a competitive advantage because our strategy in New Mexico is to build a lot of storage, gather a lot of water into that storage, connect all of our storage together.


So we have about 26,000,000 barrels of storage in New Mexico right now. Across 30 something facilities, we have about a million and a half barrels per day of treatment capacity. So we’re bringing water in all over the place, and we have the ability to move that water to wherever the frac is. So the water coming in is coming in small quantities. Thousand barrels here, 2,000 barrels there. Sometimes you’ll get a 12 well pad that’ll kick off and you might see 60,000 barrels a day coming in, but it tapers off quickly.


So the water is distributed all over the place, and our job is to pull it together, treat it so we can store it, and we’ll talk more about that later. And then we’re able through our network of 16 inch, 20 inch lines connecting all of our pits, we’re able to move the water where it’s needed and support these huge, like as you said, two trimul-fracs, 600,000 barrels per day. At one point we were supporting two trimul-fracs, and this was in January, and four other fracs and we were pushing out 1,100,000 barrels per day.


And the logistics behind that takes a lot of guys working on my team that are a lot smarter than me to figure all that out. That… That’s absolutely amazing and so much different than where we were just ten years ago. So you think that’s… That is definitely the future of where we’re headed, particularly when it comes to produced water reuse, just more and more infrastructure, more pipe underground, more connectivity. I think our… The executive team at Select that had this vision of a recycle first approach was it was disrupting in the New Mexico market.


And we all know the challenges with disposal. You know you have a really strong knowledge about the technical challenges of disposal and I’d like to hear your opinions on it. But ultimately what it means is there’s a lot less disposal capacity in New Mexico for various reasons, but the water keeps coming. The water keeps coming and it keeps coming at greater volumes. So I think a business model like ours is a part of the solution. It’s not the entire solution, but it’s a part of the solution. And a part of the solution is to take as much water as possible, gather it, store it, and then send it where it needs to go for the fracs.


What you… That type of scale is what has made Select the leader in New Mexico for treatment and reuse. The actual treatment of the water itself has become sort of commoditized when you talk about treatment for reuse on fracs. Desalinating, that’s different. But treating for reuse for fracs is a fairly simple process and us and our competitors follow pretty much the same routine. We treat it with an oxidant. We send it through… Most folks use a dissolved air flotation system. We use gases to kinda carry all the solids up to the top, and then we scrape it off the top.


Sometimes we’ll filter it a little bit more after that and we send it to the pit. So that… There are some companies out there that can do that. What companies don’t have that Select has right now in New Mexico is a combination of things. Number one, our executive team has made this strategic move to invest heavily in that infrastructure in New Mexico that we have now. So we have all these huge diameter pipelines connecting 26,000,000 barrels of storage. That storage, that size enables us to do things with water reuse that other companies simply cannot at a scale that others cannot.


The reason we were able to get to that scale, that all that technology that we’re putting, rather all the capital we’re spending on infrastructure, we have to underwrite that somehow. We have to say, okay, we’re gonna spend this money, but we know we’re gonna make money. We know we’re gonna make a return on that capital because of these revenue projections. And the way to do that is we… You have to have relationships. So you have to have trusting relationships with operators that they’ll commit to you. We’re gonna send you our water and then we’re gonna trust you to treat it and store it and then send it where we need it for our fracs.


And that trusting relationship with a few core partners is how we started all this. We said to a few of our key customers that we’re gonna put in this infrastructure and it’s gonna allow you to recycle water. And that was a leap of faith for them. The leap of faith was can Select really do what it’s saying? Reach this scale, but also connect operators water. Yes. So we will take water from eight different operators in 12 different places and we’ll send every molecule of that water to a frac for an entirely separate operator that’s 20 miles away.


And we have to because we have to… There’s not enough water coming back in any one place To support a trimul-frac. You have to gather it together. You have to move it. In order to do all that, you have to treat it first to make sure the bacteria don’t take over. And then you move it to where it needs to be. And that’s what Select has done that others haven’t, and that’s built on our trusting relationships with our partners. And then a big bet that we’re gonna spend a lot of money putting this together. Our thesis is that this is going to work, now we’re three years into it, and it’s working.


I was fixing to say, I think you’ve proved that it does work. From pipe in the ground, let’s talk about how that’s evolved over time. It’s evolved a lot and it’s evolved very quickly just recently and I’d say since COVID. So since 2020 and beyond, the pipe sizes have just increased. So what we found is before we might put eight inch, 10 inch, 12 inch, we might even get really aggressive and put a 16 inch pipe in the ground thinking maybe someday we’ll make it economic because it’s expensive to put a 16 inch pipe into the ground.


Now shift to today and Select has hundreds of miles of 16 inch pipe, hundreds of miles of 20 inch pipe. We’ve got dozens, maybe hundreds at this point of pipeline. And this is high density polyethylene pipe. It’s plastic pipe. Very thick wall plastic pipe. Very durable, very dependable. And we’re moving 100, 200, 300,000 barrels a day here and there to get the water where it needs to be. And that’s a huge change for our industry. Our business model of we’re going to put a lot of pits in the ground. We’re gonna build them right to make sure that they’re gonna hold the water the way we expect them to.


And then we’re gonna connect all of them with pipelines because we know that the fracs move and the fracs aren’t always near this one pit that we spent a million dollars building. That’s right. It’s gonna be down here 60 miles away. So we can literally today say that, for those familiar with New Mexico, we can send water from Arkansas Junction almost to Hobbs all the way down to White City where the caverns are, South of Carlsbad. We can move water from one corner of Lea County to the other corner of Eddy County. And that’s a huge change.


That is absolutely a huge change. That is quite a bit… Knowing New Mexico, that’s quite a bit of distance to move water across there. So when you have that kind of scale where you can take water from Arkansas Junction in New Mexico almost to Hobbs down to White City, which is south of Carlsbad. It’s a 60 mile straight line shot. If you follow the pipeline route, it’s probably closer to double that. So an important part of it of that infrastructure is that there needs to be a backstop. When the fracs slow down We gotta keep that water coming in.


And during those times, now we have a very, what I like to think, is a sophisticated process for balancing all of this water. And what we call balancing is mostly it’s moving water around to make sure that this pit doesn’t overflow and this pit has enough water in it to support this frac. And we move more water between our pits than either the water we bring in or the water we send out. We’re shuffling it all over the place all the time. And that’s a process we call balancing, which I have a very great staff in New Mexico that that run that process.


But to backstop that, when the fracs… When we just don’t have enough storage and there’s not enough frac activity going on to allow you to continue to bring that produced water in, so we’re not shutting in oil producing wells What you need is disposal. You’re absolutely correct. We’re doing everything in our power to move water as far and as quickly as we can to support as many hydraulic fracs we’re in, but frac schedules change. And this operator may have… We’re gonna do this one, this set here in October, and the next set’s in January.


And so you’ve gotta constantly find places for that water to go and just keep it on the move, but we do run-in the instances, every company does, to where there’s just not simply enough places to go for the water you have on hand, and we do need disposal as that back stop. But the disposal… Underground injection of saltwater is always gonna be a part of our… Of any company solution, wouldn’t you say? Absolutely. And absolutely. And we’re gonna talk some more about that here in a minute and particularly… And just so the folks are aware of stuff is, you know, Select is one of our largest areas operation is, of course, Permian Basin.


Though we are in many other basins within The US and operating. And a lot of people might know this, but for those of you that don’t, if you took that little bitty section of Southeast New Mexico and West Texas and you… We were to take it and make it its own nation, that becomes the fourth largest oil producing nation on Earth. So there’s a lot of interest on that and particularly the… What the… We believe the future is for disposal in that area. And we’ll get around to talking about that here in a minute and some of the things that are currently being done toward that end.


I’d also like to talk a little bit more. Obviously, the infrastructure is a big deal. But in the future, I think we’re gonna see a lot of opportunities where we need water coming both ways. We may treat it and send it out for a frac, but then again, we may also treat it and send it out for some other industrial use, whether it be a data center or natural gas power generation cooling or something like that. And then we may have the need, depending on where the rules end up landing, to bring the concentrate back from that cooling operation.


So Obviously, we’re pretty adept at putting pipe in the ground. We are. And what do you… Rick, what do you think about the concept that I’ve heard a lot of folks talk about and it makes a lot of sense of taking the advantages of economies of scale, gathering produced water like we do, and we have a… We are very good at gathering water together and managing it. We’re very good at putting pipe in the ground and moving water around. We’re good at treating water, technology agnostic, just depending We on what the end use don’t really sell technology.


We sell solutions, and we work with all of the water treatment technology providers to cobble together the right solution for any specific scenario. But what do you think about this idea of bringing say, let’s talk big scale here, let’s say 250,000 barrels a day To a location. We draw the fresh water off of it. Maybe we draw off, let’s just use round numbers, let’s say we draw off half of it. So we got now a 125,000 barrels per day of very nice clean fresh water that there are uses for that. You mentioned data centers.


We use it cool data centers. With data centers you’re balancing out energy or fresh water. That’s right. You’re going one way or the other. So if we can provide them fresh water, okay so you have that. Now this brine that’s left behind is concentrated. And since we have partnerships with mineral extraction companies, we’re moving very… We’re looking at a lot of different things. But right now it’s iodine and lithium. Lithium and iodine. So now you have this concentrated brine, their economics, our partners economics in mineral extraction are better.


Fresh water go into the to a use that’s gonna offset the use of critical freshwater resources in New Mexico that exist Absolutely. On the surface or in aquifers. And then we’ll take that water back, that concentrate after it’s been treated for mineral extraction, we’ll use it for fracs. So what do you see as the challenges to that vision being, you know… That that is where we’re headed eventually. There is such a demand for fresh water in Southeast New Mexico and West Texas. There always has been. I grew up just outside of Midland on a small farm, and we couldn’t drink our well water from our house.


We irrigated cotton and alfalfa with it, but we couldn’t drink it. But there will always be a need for that. And I… I’ve still got a brother and sister who live out there, and you go out there now and it’s just like anywhere else. You know, there’s reuse ponds set up everywhere, but there’s still a ton of groundwater being sold for fracs Just due to surface use agreements. The landowner owns the water underneath his land. So if you’re gonna operate on it, a lot times it’s gonna be right into the contract. You buy my water.


You gotta buy my water. That that is being addressed to some degree. I wanna step off for a minute and talk about… Currently, there’s a group called the National Petroleum Council. National Petroleum Council exist as a information source for the Department of Energy. And what… So what happens in a given scenario is the Department of Energy, the secretary or one of the two undersecretaries sends a note to the National Petroleum Council and says, I wanna know all there is to know about this. And that’s what the National Petroleum Council does.


They assemble a team. They start putting it together, and then they generate a report, and they send it back to the secretary or undersecretary. And that’s… One of those is currently underway right now focused on produced water. And I happen to be a task group lead on that and enjoying the experience very much. But a lot of that has to do with, centered around the concept of in the future, where could produced water be a hindrance to America’s energy dominance. So as you can imagine, the bull’s eyes on the Permian Basin for sure, but we’re looking at other basins as well.


That study is expected to be released to the DOE sometime in December of this year. So by sometime next year, we’ll be able to talk more about what ended up being in that report. At present, we don’t get into what we’re talking about in it or any specifics because I work what’s… I call the coordinating subcommittee, which are the worker bees. And then above that, we have the study committee, which is the CEO as a lot of the member companies. And, ultimately, we need their approval to say, yes. This report’s ready to go out.


I’m excited to see that. So, yeah, it’s a very worthy undertaking, and, hopefully, it’ll be very helpful for the Department of Energy. And we make… We’ll be making specific recommendations on how to address some of this. Now one of the things you mentioned earlier was disposal, particularly in the Permian. Now there is many… There’s independent studies have been done. I’ve seen studies done by some of the large operators in the Permian that indicate that somewhere, generally depending on which number you’re looking at, somewhere in the next three to say seven years, we’re gonna run out of disposal capacity in the Permian Basin.


Now when that happens, you essentially have one option. Start shutting in wells because you don’t have anywhere to go with water. Now, obviously, it’ll be some of the older unconventionals that are… Tend to be more water and less oil that’ll get shut in first, but we’re gonna try to avoid that at all possible. Now when we start talking about avoiding that, we’re talking about all options are on the table. First of all, we’re still gonna need disposal. We’re not gonna get away from that. But how do we best manage the current disposal that we have?


I think what what’s… What most of the, I think, general public doesn’t know is the connection between our energy independence as a nation And the management of wastewater resources. Absolutely correct. So our industry has a remarkable way of adapting and coming up with solutions. Creating solutions that five years before that no one even thought would exist. And we find ways, horizontal drilling, treating water and reusing it. We come up with amazing technology as an industry, some of the smartest people in the world.


And I have confidence in our ability to meet that that delta between what produced water is gonna be produced to give us the oil production to balance geopolitics worldwide. We have to come up with a way of managing that. And as you said, disposal has to be a part of it. It will always be a part of it. Recycling for reuse on fracs, which is what my team does, will always be a huge part of it as long as the fracs are ongoing. But we have to figure out what happens when the fracs stop in an area because eventually you drill up all the rock, you frac all the rock, and you’ve gotten the most that you can out of that area from a geographic perspective, at least for a little while.


And then what happens? Then what happens? Well… And I say this all the time. You know, when I talk about these studies, say, three to seven years, if we lost… If we shut down frac tomorrow, we don’t have enough plate. We don’t have room to go with the water we have now. Without fracs pulling that up, I believe the number of… On average, about six to 7,000,000 barrels a day are going to frac. We don’t have that room in our current disposal wells. So the fracs have to keep going. If they stop, whether we run out of rock to drill or heaven forbid we have another downturn, the oil dips down into the thirties and all of a sudden we start shutting completion crews down, then we got a problem.


Not only we’ll lose the… All the new production, the initial production from the new wells because they won’t be fracking. But we’ll also have to shut in some of the older wells because we don’t have anything to do with the produced fluid. So what do you think that solution suite looks like, let’s say five, ten years from now? I know Select is investing incredible time and money into putting this. We wanna be a part of this. We wanna be a part of solving this huge problem that impacts our energy independence as a country.


Something that I’m very passionate about having served in Iraq for, you know, what you could argue was about oil prices one way or another, at least it was related. What do you think that’s… That solution suite is going to look like beyond what we are… We’re already doing now? Like, what are the things that are gonna emerge? Now we’re getting into stuff that I’m very excited to talk about. And, you know, one of the things that we do wanna mention that, you know, obviously, everybody out there today, if you’re going to the pump, particularly if you have a diesel truck like I do and you go to the pump, you’re just like, holy cow.


$6 a gallon where I’m at, where I live. And, if America hadn’t got to this point of energy dominance and self sufficiency with energy, there’s no telling where the price of gas would be today with the Strait of Hormuz basically shut down. So thank goodness we’ve got the men and women out in the oil field that are drilling wells and completing wells and moving water and keeping things going, or else we might be looking at $8 to $10 a gallon diesel. And when you get into the numbers like that, then you start running into all these other issues like trucking starts shutting down.


That cripples the economy. Not that that’s my expertise, but it’s just common sense. If diesel prices go up to 8 or $10 That’s right. A gallon, you’re gonna have less diesel use. That means transportation being crippled. Well, so let’s talk about some of the other possibilities out there and what Select’s doing around that. And first of all, let me say, that’s a large part or at least a very good part of what I do. Very fortunate to do it in conjunction with two good friends, Nate Bonda, who was on our earlier podcast with me, and doctor Jin Hu.


And we kinda formed the, basically, the triad of evaluating… As you said, we’re technology agnostic. So if we hear of somebody that’s got a technology, we invite them to come in to talk to us, and let’s take a look at it. We’ve run a lot of pilots. And just so you know, my… I haven’t changed my spots. If they’ve got a faulty premise, I start peeling it apart. And some do. Especially in desal. So we’ve taken a look at a lot of different technologies, piloted one very successfully this past year over in the Midland Basin, just North of Midland.


We treated water that was roughly about a 120, 130,000 milligrams per liter of total dissolved solids. We produced a clean, polished distillate that was roughly 200 milligrams per liter of total dissolved solids. And we ran a irrigation pilot last year in conjunction with our operator partner and with the Texas Tech University and the Texas produced water consortium. They came down, and we set up plots, and we took five different crops, and we ended up with a total of a 120 plots. Each plot, one meter by five meters, with each plot containing a one by one square of a individual crop.


Cotton, sorghum, native grass, a grass seed that was native to the Permian back about a hundred and fifty years ago, and then a plant called, guayule. And guayule is a plant grown predominantly down, it’s a… Likes a air… Or warm climates was done a lot in, Mexico In that area. It produces a latex rubber in its structure that you can harvest out of it. Alright. And, anyway, we did that. We had a 120 plots. A third of them were irrigated with our, polished distillate. A third were irrigated with groundwater from the ranch, which, by the way, was 2,500 milligrams per liter total dissolved.


And then a third of them only got natural precipitation. We got a late start last year, but we still saw some very promising results out of it. Obviously, we would have… You know, typically, sorghum will get up a little above waist high, putting on heads and stuff like that. And we started late. We saw it about you know, most of the plants about two foot off the ground. Where it was only received natural irrigate… Natural precipitation, no growth. It just didn’t rain enough. And the same way with the grasses. Grasses flourished where we were watering them, where it got natural precipitation.


Just brown grass like we’re used to seeing. How did our irrigated crops perform against the crops irrigated with local water, a little bit higher TD… TDS water? Performed very well. As you can imagine, we did several different studies with this and in conjunction with the consortium and with Texas Tech University. You know, a lot of people… There’s a lot of concern out there by people about how do you know you got this water clean enough. We had it analyzed through a third party NELAP, National Environmental Lab Accreditation Program lab.


So we hired… We had them send out a professional sampler to make sure all the samples were caught right, went back to their lab to follow all the standard testing protocols, whether they’re your EPA procedure or ASTM procedure, And we tested for over close to 700 different analytes in that water. Everything looked much better. The… At the end of the day, we had a handful that couldn’t be fully identified, but they didn’t have a structure in them that would indicate they were toxic. But it… The same number that was in City of Midland water.


So we were very confident it was doing good. Now what Tech has done is they have taken the plants back, and they’ve looked at the cell structure in the plant. No difference in the cell structure between irrigated with either groundwater or our water. None of that. The plants were… Is healthy on either side. We did see a little better growth out of the sorghum with the groundwater, so, evidently, it prefers a salt. It was a breed… A type of sorghum that prefers a saltier water, which isn’t uncommon. Because over time in the Permian, the plants that you are available, the seeds are available to you have been migrated to deal with the type of water you’re gonna irrigate it with.


That’s alfalfa. We didn’t use alfalfa, but alfalfa is one that obviously, you know, a ton of it’s grown out in Arizona. And we grew alfalfa when I was a kid, but there’s different strains of alfalfa. Some like really fresh water, some like a saltier water. And in West Texas, it’s pretty much what we grew was a saltier. Well, I could speak a little bit to the operation side of ensuring that we only put water on the ground If that’s where we end up going. That it’s gonna be beneficial. Beneficial Right? Can speak to the operations of that.


I’ve had some experience with it over the years, distilling water, putting water through membranes. I’ve had the privilege of working with a lot of smart people who have done projects in, especially in the Marcellus you and Nate talked about. Pennsylvania, in Colorado Rockies area. And also in Arkansas when the Fayetteville Shale was going, there was a little desal project out there. So from an operational standpoint, what we would do is we’re not treating the water and sending it right into a ditch. Now that’s all theoretical at this point because this isn’t done on a commercial level in the Midland Basin.


But we’re not gonna just treat the water and send it right down a pipeline into the river or to irrigate crop crops or to a data center. What we’re gonna do is we’re gonna build a million barrel pit. And we’re gonna treat water and we’re gonna treat water into this pit. And we’re gonna let it build up. We’re gonna let it homogenize, and we’re gonna test that water. That’s right. And we’re gonna test it from the exact spot where we’re gonna pull out of it with a pump and put… And send it wherever it’s gonna go for its fresh water purpose, and that gives us some certainty.


Because we’re not gonna let that water out if it’s not meeting the stage. That’s right. And that’s one of the issues we talk about today is that when it comes to, beneficial reuse, particularly, if we talk, direct discharge, which there… We are one of the six companies or one of the five companies that have applied for permits through the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for a discharge. Five of the… There are six permits currently in the queue. Five of them are for the, Pecos River Watershed, and one of them is actually a operator that plans to discharge South of Midland I see.


Into a creek bed. But you’re absolutely right. Without the ability, which we do not have right now, without the ability to do continual monitoring for a lot of these things.
